paras: The whipping of Herman Morrison was an assault on July 16, 1903, near Bedford, Indiana, in which a group of white boys tied Morrison, a fifteen-year-old Black boy, to a tree or bush and whipped him. Mayor Smith fined each of the white boys $10.50, then fined Morrison and a white companion the same for an earlier whipping of another boy. The Indianapolis Journal called the boys "youthful whitecappers" imitating whitecappings in nearby counties.

According to a Bedford dispatch to the Indianapolis Journal, white boys and a "little colored companion" were playing near the city limits when a fight with the Black boy left one white boy with two dislocated fingers and a scratched face.

His companions, said to have heard of "the whitecappings in adjoining counties," caught the Black boy, tied him to a small tree and switched him. The Louisville Courier-Journal, which alone named him, said the boys gave Morrison "a severe whipping."

Mayor Smith, told of the affair, promised to "make it hot for the youthful whitecappers" if the account proved true. Brought before him, the boys were each fined $10.50 and given a severe lecture. At the hearing, the Journal wrote, it "developed" that the whipping answered Morrison's part, with a white companion, in tying and whipping Genie Quackenbosh (Gene Quackenbush in the Courier-Journal). Morrison and that companion, named in the Journal as Kent Seers, were then arrested and fined the same amount.

The story appears in two white dailies, each through a Bedford special; no Black-press report was found. The Journal ran it first on July 18 under "Colored Boy Is Beaten," subheaded "Youthful Bedford Whitecappers Emulate Recent Examples," and closed it on July 20 with "Youthful Whitecappers Fined." The Courier-Journal's July 21 brief, "Fined and Reprimanded For Whipping a Negro," ended on the counter-fine for the whipping "for which the negro was whitecapped."

The first Journal report traced the whipping to the fight, while the later reports, drawn from the mayor's hearing, gave the Quackenbosh whipping as the reason. No account from Morrison's side appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Whipping of Herman Morrison
bases: A group of white boys aged fourteen and fifteen tied a Black boy to a tree or bush and whipped him after a quarrel (A1, A3); the papers called them 'youthful whitecappers' imitating whitecapping elsewhere, but no organized band, warning or night raid is reported (A1, A2).

Two Bedford specials to different papers, the Indianapolis Journal (A1, A2) and the Louisville Courier-Journal (A3), agree on the tying and whipping, the mayor's fines and the counter-fine, though both follow the outcome in the mayor's court.

accounts.label: First Bedford dispatch
accounts.gist: A fight between the Black boy and one white boy left the white boy hurt; his companions, having heard of whitecappings in adjoining counties, tied the Black boy to a small tree and switched him.

accounts.label: Mayor's court
accounts.gist: The hearing 'developed' that the whipping was for the Black boy's part, with a white companion, in tying and whipping Genie Quackenbosh; both sets of boys were fined $10.50.

framing.detail: The Indianapolis Journal headlined 'Colored Boy Is Beaten' and 'Youthful Bedford Whitecappers Emulate Recent Examples,' then 'Youthful Whitecappers Fined,' treating it as a juvenile 'escapade' the mayor would 'make it hot' for.
The Courier-Journal's brief 'Fined and Reprimanded For Whipping a Negro' said Morrison was 'whitecapped' for the earlier whipping, ending on the counter-fine.
